items.title: 9.1 Anatomy and physiology of the digestive system

source_refs.note: Chapter opening and the single topic 9.1, printed pages 202-212: the GI tract from mouth to anus, the accessory organs, motility, the control of secretions, absorption and the liver's roles. Figures 9.1 to 9.8 are carried by six schematic originals.

blocks.text: Digestion is the process by which the body breaks down food into smaller, absorbable components. It is crucial for converting food into energy and the raw materials required for growth, repair and the maintenance of body functions; it supports the immune system, provides essential nutrients and ensures overall health. Efficient digestion prevents nutrient deficiencies, supports metabolism and maintains energy levels, making it vital for sustaining life.

The human digestive system is composed of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract and the accessory digestive organs. The GI tract is a continuous tube that extends from mouth to anus: the oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. The accessory digestive organs are the salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas.

blocks.alt: An outline of the head and trunk showing the gut from mouth to anus: Tongue, Salivary glands, Pharynx, Oesophagus, Stomach, the Small intestine (Duodenum, Jejunum, Ileum) and the Colon (Transverse colon, Ascending colon, Descending colon), with the Cecum, Appendix, Rectum and Anus. The Liver, Gallbladder and Pancreas lie by the stomach; the Common bile duct and Pancreatic duct join the duodenum.

blocks.text: Oral cavity

The oral cavity is the cavity immediately after the opening of the mouth. The lips are made of highly vascularised skeletal muscle tissue with many sensory nerve endings; they help to retain food as it is chewed and also play a role in phonation, the modification of sound. The oral cavity performs three important functions.

items: Selection of food: the muscular tongue plays its role in selecting food through its taste buds. When food enters the oral cavity it is tasted and physically felt; if the taste or smell is unpleasant, or hard objects such as bone or dirt are present, it is rejected. The senses of smell and sight also take part in the selection of food.

Mechanical digestion: the ingested food is physically broken down by the teeth in mastication (chewing). Chewing reduces food to smaller, more manageable pieces, increasing the surface area for enzymatic action.
Chemical digestion: as chewing goes on, the salivary glands pour their secretion, saliva, into the oral cavity, and the palate, tongue and cheeks help to mix the chewed food with it.

blocks.text: There are three pairs of salivary glands: the sublingual glands below the tongue, the submaxillary glands behind the jaws, and the parotid glands in front of the ears. Saliva contains water and mucus that moisten and lubricate the food, bicarbonate ions that buffer chemicals in the oral cavity, and thiocyanate ions that kill microorganisms. Fresh saliva is alkaline (pH 8) but quickly loses CO2 and reaches pH 6. It also contains the enzyme salivary amylase, which partially digests the polysaccharides starch and glycogen to the disaccharide maltose. After the mechanical and chemical processes of the oral cavity, the food is a small moist mass called a bolus.

blocks.alt: A side view of the head. The Parotid gland lies in front of and below the ear, with its duct running forward to the mouth; the Submaxillary gland lies below the angle of the jaw; the Sublingual gland lies in the floor of the mouth under the tongue.

blocks.text: Pharynx and swallowing

The pharynx is the cavity behind the mouth and the common passageway of the digestive and respiratory tracts. The bolus is pushed to the back of the mouth and swallowed through the pharynx. During swallowing the tongue moves upwards and backwards against the roof of the mouth, forcing the bolus to the back of the oral cavity, and the soft palate is raised against the back wall of the pharynx; these movements close the passage between the nasal cavity and the pharynx. At the same time the larynx moves upward, which lowers the epiglottis, a flap of cartilage, and closes the opening of the trachea. In this way the bolus passes over the trachea and enters the oesophagus.

blocks.title: Voluntary, then automatic
blocks.text: The beginning of the swallowing action is voluntary, but once the food reaches the back of the mouth, swallowing becomes automatic.

blocks.alt: Three section views of the head and neck. First: the Soft palate elevated against back wall of pharynx, the Bolus at the back of the mouth, and the Tongue moves upwards and backwards. Second: the Epiglottis lowers to close glottis while the Larynx moves upwards, and the bolus passes over the windpipe. Third: the bolus is in the oesophagus, the Soft palate relaxes and the Epiglottis raises.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.3: Swallowing of food (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.3).

blocks.text: Oesophagus

After being swallowed, the food enters the oesophagus, the tube that connects the pharynx to the stomach; the digestive action of saliva continues in it. In an adult the oesophagus is about 25 cm long and its lower end opens into the stomach. Food moves down to the stomach by peristalsis. The exit of food into the stomach is controlled by the lower oesophageal sphincter or cardiac sphincter, which opens in response to the pressure exerted by food and prevents the backflow of stomach contents into the oesophagus.

blocks.alt: A long tube, the Oesophagus, with a Bolus inside, opening through the Cardiac sphincter into the Stomach; from the lower left end of the stomach the Small intestine begins.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.4: Oesophagus and its connections (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.4).

blocks.text: Motility of the alimentary canal

items: Peristalsis is the rhythmic sequence of waves of contraction in the smooth muscles of the walls of the alimentary canal. It squeezes the food along the oesophagus and the other parts of the canal.

Segmentation: the small and large intestines also have rings of smooth muscle that contract and relax repeatedly, creating a back-and-forth movement in the same place. This mixes the food with the digestive secretions and increases the efficiency of absorption.

blocks.text: Occasionally the peristaltic movements reverse, in antiperistalsis, pushing food from the intestines back into the stomach and oral cavity and leading to vomiting. In contrast, hunger contractions are peristaltic movements triggered by low blood glucose, creating the uncomfortable sensation known as hunger pangs.

blocks.alt: The oesophagus with a bolus: the muscle ring behind the bolus is contracted (Muscles contracted) and the part ahead is relaxed (Muscles relaxed); a large arrow shows Peristalsis downward. The oesophagus opens through the Cardiac sphincter into the Stomach, with a curved Peristalsis arrow along it, and the stomach empties through the Pyloric sphincter into the Small intestine, where rings show Segmentation movements.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.5: Peristalsis and Segmentation (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.5).

blocks.title: Heartburn
blocks.text: Sometimes acidic chyme flushes back from the stomach into the oesophagus. It causes a painful burning sensation in the chest, a condition known as pyrosis or heartburn.
The stomach

The stomach is an elastic, muscular, J-shaped bag situated after the oesophagus and before the duodenum, on the left side of the abdominal cavity right below the diaphragm. It has three portions: the cardiac portion immediately after the oesophagus, the fundus on one side of the cardiac portion, and the pyloric portion beneath the cardiac portion. The cardiac sphincter opens when a wave of peristaltic contractions coming down the oesophagus reaches it, and lets food enter the stomach.
Mechanical digestion in the stomach

The stomach wall is made of the same layers as the other parts of the alimentary canal: the outermost serosa, a middle layer of smooth muscle, and the inner two layers, submucosa and mucosa. In the stomach the muscle has three layers, outer longitudinal, middle circular and inner oblique. The muscular walls contract vigorously, churning the food (mechanical digestion) and mixing it with the stomach secretions; these contractions also generate enough heat to melt solid fats.
Chemical digestion in the stomach

The mucosa of the stomach possesses numerous tubular gastric glands, which open into the mucosa through deep depressions called gastric pits. Each gland contains epithelial cells and three kinds of secretory cell.

items: The mucous cells secrete mucus, a thick secretion that covers the inside of the stomach and protects it from HCl and the digestive enzymes.
The parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete hydrochloric acid, which adjusts the pH of the stomach contents to about 2 to 3. HCl also softens the food, activates pepsinogen and kills microorganisms.
The chief cells secrete the enzyme pepsinogen.

blocks.alt: A J-shaped stomach with the oesophagus entering at the Cardiac portion, the dome-like Fundus portion and the Pyloric portion ending in a ring. A cut-away band shows the wall layers: Serosa, Longitudinal muscles, Circular muscles, Oblique muscles, Submucosa and Mucosa. An arrow leads to a block of Mucosa with gastric glands, and another to one Gastric pit and Gastric gland lined with cells; arrows pick out the Epithelial cell, Mucous cell, Parietal cell and Chief cell.

blocks.text: All the secretions of the gastric glands together are the gastric juice. When the bolus enters the stomach the glands secrete gastric juice; the H+ ions of the HCl activate pepsinogen into pepsin, and pepsin catalyses the breakdown of proteins into polypeptides and peptides. About three to four hours after a meal the stomach contents have been sufficiently mixed and are a semi-liquid acidic mass called chyme. The pyloric sphincter regulates the release of chyme into the small intestine.

blocks.title: Rennin in infants
blocks.text: In infants the gastric juice contains large amounts of the enzyme rennin, which coagulates milk proteins and delays the passage of milk into the small intestine, so that the other enzymes have time to digest the milk proteins.

blocks.title: How the stomach protects itself
blocks.text: The mucosa of the stomach would be damaged by acid and pepsin if it had no protection. It is protected in two ways: by viscous mucus, and by bicarbonate, which neutralises acid.
Regulation of the secretion of gastric juice

The secretion of gastric juice is regulated by both the nervous system and hormones. In reaction to the smell, sight or thought of food, the medulla of the brain sends a message to the gastric glands to secrete small amounts of gastric juice. When food arrives, the distension of the stomach and the fall in the pH of its contents stimulate more secretion and powerful contractions. The presence of proteins in the food stimulates special endocrine cells in the mucosa to release the hormone gastrin, which is carried by the blood to the gastric glands and stimulates them to produce and secrete more gastric juice. When the food moves from the stomach to the small intestine, the hormone somatostatin stops the release of hydrochloric acid.
The small intestine

The small intestine is the longest part of the alimentary canal, starting after the stomach and ending at the large intestine; in an adult it is about 2 to 3 cm in diameter and 6 m long. It is responsible not only for the final digestion of all kinds of food but also for the absorption of the digested food into blood and lymph. It has three parts: the duodenum, jejunum and ileum.
Duodenum

The first 20 to 25 cm is the duodenum, which is concerned with the digestion of food. It contains glands that produce an alkaline secretion containing bicarbonate, and two main secretions are poured into it: pancreatic juice and bile. Pancreatic juice, the secretion of the pancreas, is slightly alkaline (pH 8) because of its bicarbonate and neutralises the acidity of the chyme. Its important enzymes are listed below.

items: Pancreatic amylase digests polysaccharides into maltose and even glucose.
Trypsinogen is secreted in an inactive form; the enzyme enterokinase, secreted by the walls of the duodenum, activates it into trypsin, which digests proteins into polypeptides.
Chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase digest proteins into smaller peptides and then into amino acids.
Pancreatic lipase digests lipids to glycerol and fatty acids.
Pancreatic nucleases digest DNA and RNA into nucleotides.

blocks.text: Bile is the secretion of the liver, stored in the gallbladder before release. It contains salts that emulsify fats, breaking them into small droplets (an emulsion) that provide a large surface area for the effective action of the lipid-digesting enzymes.

blocks.title: Why bile is needed, and jaundice
blocks.text: Fats are insoluble in water, so the lipase of the pancreatic juice cannot attack them readily. Bile salts act as detergent molecules: they break fats into droplets and keep the droplets separate from one another. If the bile pigments are prevented from leaving the digestive tract they may accumulate in the blood, causing the condition known as jaundice.
Jejunum and ileum

The jejunum, 2.4 metres long, follows the duodenum, and the ileum, the last three fifths and about 3.5 metres long, completes the small intestine. These parts carry out the rest of digestion and the absorption of food. Their walls contain glands that secrete intestinal juice, whose enzymes are listed in the table. After the action of these enzymes the chyme is converted into an alkaline emulsion called chyle.
Absorption of digested food and water

The absorption of digested food, water and dissolved minerals takes place in the jejunum and ileum. Their inner wall has large circular folds bearing numerous finger-like projections called villi, so the internal surface looks velvety. Each villus is richly supplied with blood capillaries and with a vessel of the lymphatic system called a lacteal, all covered by an epithelium one cell thick. The epithelial cells carry countless cytoplasmic projections, the microvilli. Because of the villi and microvilli the total surface area for absorption becomes extraordinarily large.

items: Simple sugars and amino acids: glucose and the amino acids are absorbed by diffusion or active transport into the epithelial cells of the villi and from there enter the blood capillaries, which join to form the hepatic portal vein carrying them to the liver. The liver stores extra glucose and amino acids as glycogen and proteins, and the required amounts pass from the liver to the heart through the hepatic vein.

Fatty acids and glycerol: the products of fat digestion are absorbed by passive transport into the epithelial cells, where they recombine into triglycerides. The triglycerides are coated with proteins to form small droplets called chylomicrons, which enter the lacteals, move into the thoracic lymphatic duct and from there into the bloodstream. Blood plasma has enzymes that hydrolyse the chylomicrons back into fats and proteins; the fats are finally hydrolysed into fatty acids and glycerol and enter the body cells.

blocks.text: The large intestine

The large intestine is the last part of the alimentary canal, much shorter than the small intestine and occupying about the last metre of the tract. It absorbs water, salts and vitamin K from the lumen into the blood. It is not convoluted and its inner surface has no villi. It consists of three parts.

items: Cecum: a blind sac projecting from the large intestine between the ileum and the colon. From its blind end arises a finger-like process, the vermiform appendix, which performs no function in the human digestive system and is vestigial.

Colon: next to the cecum, with an ascending, a transverse and a descending limb. Its main function is to absorb water from the alimentary canal; as water is absorbed the remaining material becomes more solid. These wastes, the faeces, consist of a large number of bacteria, indigestible plant fibres such as cellulose, other undigested food, sloughed-off mucosal cells, bile pigments and water.

Rectum: the last part of the large intestine, where faeces are stored temporarily. It opens out through the anus, which is surrounded by two sphincters: the internal sphincter of smooth muscle and the outer of striated muscle. When the rectum fills with faeces a defecation reflex arises; it is consciously inhibited in adults but involuntary in infants, and during growth the child learns to bring it under voluntary control.

blocks.title: Appendicitis
blocks.text: Appendicitis is the inflammation of the appendix, usually due to bacterial infection. The infected appendix must be removed surgically, otherwise it may burst and the inflammation may spread through the entire lining of the abdomen. The surgical removal of the appendix is appendicectomy.

Many bacteria, for example E. coli, live and actively divide in the colon. During their metabolism they produce amino acids and vitamin K, which is necessary for the coagulation of blood and is absorbed from the large intestine into the blood.
Control of egestion

The involuntary reflex for egestion in infants and the voluntary control in adults represent two stages of neurological and muscular development. In infants egestion is an involuntary reflex mediated by the spinal cord: distension of the rectum triggers automatic relaxation of the internal anal sphincter and expulsion of waste, because the higher brain centres responsible for voluntary control are not yet fully developed. In adults egestion becomes voluntary as the cerebral cortex matures, allowing conscious regulation of the external anal sphincter to delay or initiate defecation. This transition reflects the integration of reflex pathways with cognitive control, adapting to social and environmental demands.
Accessory digestive organs

items: Liver and gallbladder: the liver produces bile, which is essential for fat digestion because it emulsifies fats. The liver also processes the nutrients absorbed from the small intestine, detoxifies harmful substances, synthesises proteins and stores glycogen for energy. The gallbladder stores and concentrates the bile; when food enters the small intestine it releases bile through the bile duct.

Pancreas: a large gland just ventral to the stomach with exocrine and endocrine portions. The exocrine (ducted) portion secretes pancreatic juice into the pancreatic duct, which joins the common bile duct from the liver and enters the duodenum; the juice contains enzymes for all groups of food, chiefly trypsin, chymotrypsin, lipases, amylases and nucleases. The endocrine (ductless) portion secretes the hormones insulin and glucagon into the extracellular fluid, from where they diffuse into nearby capillaries.

blocks.title: Gall stones
blocks.text: Cholesterol secreted by the liver may precipitate in the gallbladder to produce gall stones, which may block the release of bile.
Hormonal control of the secretions of the pancreas and liver

The release of secretions from the pancreas and liver is also controlled by hormones. When chyme enters the duodenum from the stomach, its acidity stimulates the duodenal walls to release the hormone secretin. Similarly, the partially digested proteins and fats in the chyme stimulate the duodenal walls to secrete another hormone, cholecystokinin (CCK). Both hormones stimulate the pancreas to release pancreatic juice and the gallbladder to release bile.

blocks.alt: The Liver above the Stomach and Spleen, with the Gallbladder under the liver. The Right hepatic duct and Left hepatic duct join as the Common hepatic duct, which meets the Cystic duct from the gallbladder to form the Common bile duct running to the Duodenum (first part of small intestine). The Pancreas lies in the curve of the duodenum. The Hepatic portal vein and Hepatic artery run to the liver.

blocks.text: Storage and metabolic role of the liver

The liver stores excess nutrients from the food and releases them when the body needs energy or building materials: glucose stored as glycogen, vitamins such as A, D, B12 and K, minerals such as iron and copper, and fats and fat-soluble substances. It also plays a central role in metabolism, breaking down, building up and converting substances. It converts excess glucose into glycogen and back when needed; it breaks down fats to produce energy and forms cholesterol and lipoproteins; it converts amino acids and removes harmful ammonia by turning it into urea, which is excreted in the urine; it breaks down and removes toxins, drugs and alcohol from the blood; and it helps to break down and regulate hormones.
